title: Three Friends Bet on Kulhad Chai. Now Their Brand Crosses Rs 100 Crore
excerpt: Indore's Chai Sutta Bar grew from a ₹3 lakh first shop to 600+ outlets and ₹100 crore-plus turnover — bootstrapped, franchise-led, and built on ₹10 kulhad chai.
body:
• Chai Sutta Bar — founded in June 2016 in Indore by friends Anubhav Dubey, Anand Nayak and Rahul Patidar — has grown to 600+ outlets across 370+ Indian cities, with international stores in Dubai, Oman and Nepal.
  • The brand's reported turnover is over ₹100 crore, with newer estimates near ₹150 crore — built without any external funding.
  • The first outlet opened near a girls' hostel in Indore's Bhawarkua area for just ₹3 lakh; the concept: kulhad (clay-cup) chai in a bar-style setting — no alcohol, no smoking.
  • Chai starts at ₹10 — "a brand for the masses, not the classes" — and the chain reportedly serves 4.5 lakh kulhad teas daily, supporting around 500 potter families.

Three friends from Indore bet that India's cheapest beverage could be its biggest business idea. A decade later, Chai Sutta Bar — founded in June 2016 by Anubhav Dubey, Anand Nayak and Rahul Patidar — has grown to more than 600 outlets across 370-plus cities in India, with international stores in Dubai, Oman and Nepal, and a reported turnover north of ₹100 crore. It did all of this bootstrapped: no external investment, ever.

The ₹3 lakh bet

Anubhav Dubey, then 22, came from a lower-middle-class family in Rewa, Madhya Pradesh, and had tried UPSC preparation in Delhi before moving to Indore for college. With his friends, he opened the first Chai Sutta Bar near a girls' hostel in the Bhawarkua area — total cost: ₹3 lakh. The concept was a twist on the tea stall: kulhad chai served in a bar-style setting, aimed squarely at young customers. The name itself is the joke — "Sutta" breaks replaced by "Chai" breaks.

"Chai starts at ₹10 — "a brand for the masses, not the classes" — and the chain reportedly serves 4.5 lakh kulhad teas daily , supporting around 500 potter families."

Kulhad as differentiator

The clay cup is the brand's moat. Kulhad chai costs the same to serve but tastes different — earthier, more aromatic — and it gave the founders a story no multinational could copy: every cup supports the potter families who make them. The chain now reportedly uses around 3 lakh kulhads a day, working with some 500 potter families, and has turned sustainability into a business asset rather than a cost centre.

The franchise machine

Growth came through franchising. Of the 600-plus outlets, only a handful are company-owned; the rest run on a franchise-owner-franchisee-operated (FOFO) model, supplied by a centralized master kitchen in Indore. The menu stays deliberately accessible: Adrak, Masala, Elaichi, Tulsi, Kesar and chocolate chai from ₹10, plus snacks — sandwiches, pasta, noodles, burgers, pizza. Dubey, who was named Entrepreneur of the Year (Entrepreneur Magazine India, 2021) and made the Top 30 Under 30 list in 2020, has described the brand as "for the masses, not the classes" — and the unit economics of a ₹10 hero product keep franchisees interested.

The numbers, with caveats

Revenue figures vary by source and date — older reports cite ₹100 crore-plus in cumulative turnover reached within six years; newer ones put current turnover near ₹150 crore. Outlet counts have moved from the low hundreds to 600-plus over the same period. What is consistent across all reporting: the scale was built without outside capital, on franchise fees, centralized supply, and one of the cheapest price points in organized Indian food retail.

Diaspora angle

For the diaspora, Chai Sutta Bar matters two ways: its Dubai and Oman outlets are already familiar to Gulf Indians, and its playbook — franchise-led, capital-light, built on a culturally rooted product — is a template for the Indian-food brands now opening across North America and the Middle East. The humble kulhad turns out to scale better than most venture-backed concepts.
